questions.q: Which is NOT a feature of innate immunity?
opts: Rapid response occurring within minutes to hours
Memory response upon re-exposure to antigen
Physical barriers including skin and mucus
questions.exp: Memory is a hallmark of ADAPTIVE immunity, not innate. Innate is rapid but non-specific and has no memory.

questions.q: Which innate immune cell is the FIRST to be recruited to a site of bacterial infection?
questions.exp: Neutrophils are the first to arrive at acute bacterial infections via margination, rolling, adhesion, diapedesis.
optExp: Macrophages are tissue-resident and early but neutrophils swarm rapidly from blood.
DCs sample antigen and migrate to lymph nodes.

questions.q: Which innate immune cell is primarily responsible for early antiviral defence and killing virus-infected cells?
questions.exp: NK cells recognise infected/transformed cells lacking MHC I and kill them via perforin/granzymes — innate antiviral.
optExp: Macrophages are tissue-resident phagocytes, but NK cells lead early antiviral killing.

questions.q: Mast cells release histamine, causing:
opts: Cause vasodilation and increased vascular permeability
questions.exp: Histamine causes vasodilation (redness, warmth) and increased vascular permeability (oedema) — the cardinal signs of acute inflammation.
optExp: Bronchoconstriction is one effect but not the main here.
Hypotension can occur but not the defining inflammatory effect.
Histamine triggers, not reduces, immune response.

questions.q: Lysozyme (in tears, saliva) is most effective against:
questions.exp: Lysozyme cleaves bonds in peptidoglycan, abundant in Gram-positive cell walls.
optExp: Gram-negative have thinner peptidoglycan and outer membrane (less affected).

questions.q: The complement system's three pathways converge on activation of:
questions.exp: All three pathways (classical, lectin, alternative) generate C3 convertase, which splits C3 into C3a and C3b.

questions.q: The classical complement pathway is activated by:
questions.exp: C1q binds the Fc region of antibody (IgG or IgM) bound to antigen, initiating the cascade.
optExp: Lectins drive lectin pathway, not classical.

questions.q: The alternative complement pathway is activated by:
opts: Spontaneous C3 hydrolysis and pathogen surfaces
questions.exp: C3 spontaneously hydrolyses; the resulting C3b can attach to bacterial surfaces (especially LPS), amplifying complement.

questions.q: Membrane attack complex (MAC) consists of:
opts: C5b, C6, C7, C8, and C9 proteins
C1, C2, C3, and C4 proteins
questions.exp: MAC = C5b + C6 + C7 + C8 + (multiple) C9, forming a pore that lyses pathogens (especially Gram-negative bacteria).
optExp: These are cleavage products, not the MAC.

questions.q: C3b functions as a(n):
opts: Opsonin that tags pathogens for phagocytosis
Anaphylatoxin that triggers mast cell degranulation
Chemotactic factor that attracts immune cells
questions.exp: C3b binds pathogen surfaces, marking them for phagocyte recognition (opsonisation).
optExp: C5a is the main chemotactic factor.

questions.q: C5a primarily functions as a:
questions.exp: C5a is a potent chemotactic factor and anaphylatoxin, recruiting neutrophils to the site of infection.

questions.q: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are an example of:
questions.exp: TLRs recognise pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) — defining feature of innate PRR-mediated recognition.

questions.q: C4 deficiency is most associated with:
questions.exp: C4 deficiency impairs immune complex clearance and is strongly associated with SLE (~90% develop the disease).

questions.q: Defensins and cathelicidins are:
questions.exp: Defensins/cathelicidins are AMPs secreted by neutrophils and epithelial cells, disrupting microbial membranes.

questions.q: Diapedesis refers to:
opts: Migration of leukocytes through vessel walls into tissue
questions.exp: Diapedesis is the leukocyte step of squeezing through endothelial junctions to enter tissues.
optExp: Class switching is in B cells.

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin is the primary antibody of mucosal immunity (gut, respiratory tract)?
questions.exp: IgA is secreted onto mucosal surfaces (gut, airways, breast milk) and protects against pathogens entering through these routes.
optExp: IgG is the main serum antibody.
IgD is on B cell receptors.

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin crosses the placenta to provide passive immunity to the fetus?
questions.exp: IgG is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta via FcRn receptors, giving newborns passive immunity.

questions.q: The first antibody produced in a primary immune response is:
questions.exp: IgM is the first antibody produced in response to a new antigen (primary response).

questions.q: IgE is most associated with:
opts: Type I hypersensitivity and parasitic infections
questions.exp: IgE binds mast cells and eosinophils. Crosslinking by allergen/antigen triggers degranulation — allergic and antiparasitic responses.

questions.q: MHC class I molecules:
opts: Present endogenous antigens to CD4+ T cells
questions.exp: MHC I is on all nucleated cells, presenting intracellular (endogenous) antigens to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.
optExp: MHC I downregulation occurs in some viral infections, but they are normally present.

questions.q: MHC class II molecules:
opts: Present endogenous antigens to CD8+ T cells
questions.exp: MHC II is on APCs (DCs, macrophages, B cells) and presents extracellular antigens to CD4+ helper T cells.
optExp: MHC II is restricted to APCs.
MHC I activates CD8+ T cells.

questions.q: T cells develop and mature in the:
questions.exp: T cells originate in bone marrow but migrate to the thymus where positive and negative selection occur.
optExp: LNs are sites of activation, not maturation.
Peyer's patches are gut-associated lymphoid tissue.

questions.q: Positive selection of T cells occurs in:
questions.exp: In the thymic cortex, T cells that can bind self-MHC survive ('positive selection'); those that can't undergo death by neglect.
optExp: B cells select in bone marrow.
Not the site of T cell selection.

questions.q: Negative selection of T cells eliminates:
opts: Self-reactive T cells that bind strongly to self-antigens
T cells failing to recognize self-MHC molecules
All immature T cells regardless of specificity
B cells accidentally located in the thymus
questions.exp: In the thymic medulla, T cells with high affinity for self-antigens are deleted, preventing autoimmunity.
optExp: That happens via positive selection failure (death by neglect).
Only ~2% survive selection but not all are deleted.
B cells select in bone marrow.

questions.q: CD4+ T cells differentiate into all EXCEPT:
questions.exp: CD4+ helper T cells differentiate into TH1, TH2, TH17, Treg, etc. CD8+ cytotoxic is a separate lineage.

questions.q: The variable region of an antibody:
opts: Responsible for effector functions via Fc region
Shows structural similarity across all antibody types
questions.exp: The variable regions of light and heavy chains form the antigen-binding paratope, giving each antibody its specificity.
optExp: Variable regions vary; constant is shared by isotype.

questions.q: Class switching of antibodies occurs in:
opts: T cells in secondary lymphoid organs
Activated B cells in germinal centres
questions.exp: Activated B cells undergo class switch recombination from IgM/IgD to IgG, IgA, or IgE, driven by cytokines and CD40-CD40L.
optExp: Plasma cells already produced antibody — switching happens before.

questions.q: Memory cells provide:
opts: Faster and stronger immune response on re-exposure
Direct activation of the complement cascade
questions.exp: Memory B and T cells persist after infection and mount a faster, larger response on re-encounter — basis of vaccination.

questions.q: Plasma cells are derived from:
questions.exp: Activated B cells differentiate into plasma cells, which are dedicated antibody factories.
optExp: T cells don't differentiate into plasma cells.

questions.q: Hypersensitivity Type I (allergic) is mediated by:
opts: IgG and IgM antibodies against cell antigens
IgE antibodies bound to mast cells and basophils
questions.exp: Type I: IgE binds mast cells; allergen crosslinks IgE, triggering rapid degranulation (anaphylaxis, asthma).
optExp: Complement deficiency is a different disorder.

questions.q: Type II hypersensitivity (cytotoxic) is exemplified by:
questions.exp: Type II: antibodies bind cells, activating complement or ADCC (e.g. AIHA, Goodpasture's, transfusion reactions).

questions.q: Type III hypersensitivity involves:
opts: IgE antibodies and mast cell degranulation
Immune complex deposition in blood vessels and tissues
questions.exp: Type III: antigen-antibody complexes deposit in vessels/tissues, activating complement (e.g. SLE, serum sickness, post-strep GN).

questions.q: Type IV hypersensitivity is mediated by:
questions.exp: Type IV (delayed) is T-cell mediated — TB skin test, contact dermatitis, granuloma formation.
optExp: NK cells are not the main mediator.

questions.q: A patient develops urticaria and bronchospasm minutes after a bee sting. This is which type of hypersensitivity?
questions.exp: Rapid IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation = Type I (anaphylaxis).
optExp: Type II involves antibody against cells.
No standard 'Type V' in this scheme.

questions.q: Eosinophils are especially important against:
questions.exp: Eosinophils release major basic protein and ECP, killing helminths. They also contribute to allergic inflammation.
optExp: NK cells and T cells fight viruses.

questions.q: Basophils release:
questions.exp: Basophils (and mast cells) release histamine and heparin granules in allergic responses.

questions.q: Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) recognise antigen presented on:
opts: Both MHC class I and II equally
questions.exp: CD8+ T cells recognise endogenous peptides on MHC I expressed by virtually all nucleated cells.

questions.q: B cell receptor (BCR) is essentially a membrane-bound form of:
questions.exp: BCR is a membrane-anchored immunoglobulin (initially IgM/IgD), with similar antigen-binding specificity as secreted antibodies.
optExp: TCR is a different receptor on T cells.

questions.q: Vaccination provides which type of immunity?
questions.exp: Vaccination = active artificial immunity — the immune system mounts its own response to a controlled antigen exposure, creating memory.

questions.q: Passive immunity from breast milk is mediated mainly by:
questions.exp: Secretory IgA in colostrum and breast milk provides mucosal protection to the infant's gut.
optExp: IgG crosses placenta but not main in milk.

questions.q: A patient with recurrent Neisseria meningitidis infections likely has a deficiency in:
questions.exp: Recurrent Neisseria infections suggest MAC (C5-C9) deficiency — MAC is critical for lysing Gram-negative organisms.
optExp: C3 deficiency causes severe pyogenic infections, not specifically Neisseria.
IgG deficiency causes recurrent encapsulated bacteria.

questions.q: Affinity maturation of antibodies occurs via:
opts: V(D)J recombination during B cell development
Phagocytosis of pathogens by B cells
questions.exp: Somatic hypermutation in germinal centres of lymph nodes selects B cells with higher antibody affinity for repeated exposure.
optExp: Allelic exclusion is for one allele expression.
V(D)J creates initial diversity but not affinity maturation per se.

questions.q: Interferons are mainly important against:
questions.exp: Type I interferons (α, β) are key antiviral cytokines, inducing antiviral state in neighbouring cells.

questions.q: T regulatory cells (Tregs) function to:
opts: Suppress immune response and maintain tolerance
questions.exp: Tregs (CD4+CD25+FOXP3+) dampen immune responses and prevent autoimmunity.

questions.q: The most abundant white blood cell in healthy adults is:
questions.exp: Neutrophils make up 50-70% of circulating WBCs; lymphocytes ~20-40%; monocytes ~2-10%; eosinophils ~1-4%; basophils <1%.

questions.q: Pentameric structure with 10 antigen-binding sites is a feature of:
questions.exp: Serum IgM is a pentamer (5 monomers, 10 binding sites), making it highly avid and effective at complement activation.

questions.q: Macrophages in liver are specifically called:
questions.exp: Kupffer cells are liver-resident macrophages lining sinusoids. Microglia = brain, Langerhans = skin, osteoclasts = bone, alveolar = lung.
